nodes.label: sensor_hub task — sole owner of the I2C bus
nodes.rationale: Core 1, priority 22, 4096 BYTES of stack. Only sensor_hub calls *_driver_read() — not merely for architectural tidiness: QMC5883P clears its DRDY flag the moment STATUS is read, so two readers steal each other's samples and both see intermittent data. Mahony, calibration and telemetry all read the snapshot instead.

nodes.label: stabilize_task — the entire flight control loop
nodes.rationale: Core 1, priority 23, 4096 BYTES, woken by xTaskNotifyGive from the hub with vTaskDelayUntil at 250Hz as fallback. Runs Mahony, estimator, FSM, Commander, takeoff/hold/land, mixer and motor output — and never touches I2C.

nodes.label: Why stabilize is priority 23 and not 24
nodes.rationale: 24 would tie with ipc1, core 1's own IPC task. Equal priority means round-robin, and esp_ipc_call* is the SYNCHRONOUS cross-core path IDF uses internally (e.g. allocating an interrupt for the other core) with the caller BLOCKED until the ipc task finishes. At 23 the flight loop already preempts every other task on core 1, so 24 buys nothing and only adds a hard-to-reason-about interaction to the safety core. sensor_hub at 22 ties with esp_timer, which is harmless because esp_timer is pinned to CPU0 and equal priorities only round-robin within one core. Three invariants are enforced by _Static_assert rather than comments, and the hub's priority lives in sensor_hub.h (not the .c) precisely so flight_core.c can assert against it — two numbers in two files with nothing forcing them to agree is exactly the class of bug that only surfaces in flight.

nodes.label: ESP-IDF task stack is measured in BYTES (documentation correction)
nodes.rationale: xTaskCreate/xTaskCreatePinnedToCore in ESP-IDF take stack in BYTES, deliberately differing from vanilla FreeRTOS where usStackDepth is in words. An earlier revision of this document said '4096 w = 16KB' for both flight tasks — wrong by exactly 4x. Not harmless: that figure is what people use to decide 'plenty of stack left, add a local buffer', and sensor_snapshot_t plus the per-tick structs live on those very stacks.

nodes.label: cfg.i2c_freq_hz was a dead field (fixed)
nodes.rationale: main.c and fc_bridge.c set cfg.i2c_freq_hz but flight_core never read it; the real speed came from four separate 400000 constants each driver #defined itself. Editing BOARD_I2C_FREQ_HZ did nothing — a config that looked authoritative but controlled nothing. The four copies were deleted and flight_core_start() now validates 10k..1M, logging clearly and falling back to 400000 rather than letting add_device() fail silently at 0 Hz. Note that I2C frequency is a DEVICE property, not a bus property, in the new master API: i2c_master_bus_config_t has no frequency field, it lives in i2c_device_config_t.scl_speed_hz per i2c_master_bus_add_device() — which is why it must be threaded down into every driver.

nodes.label: sensor_hub sub-rate interleaving with phase offsets
nodes.rationale: The hub runs at 250Hz but does not read all four sensors every cycle: bunching them makes one cycle's bus occupancy spike and delays the next cycle's IMU sample. IMU divisor 1 (250Hz, the clock source); MAG divisor 5 (~50Hz, higher rates are pointless against the chip ODR); BARO divisor 5 phase-offset 2 (~50Hz, matching P x8 + IIR x8, offset so it never lands on the same cycle as mag); battery divisor 25 (~10Hz, chosen because load sag happens within ~100ms and sampling every 200ms could miss the very dip the battery failsafe needs); ToF divisor 8 phase-offset 4 (~25Hz, since a 33ms timing budget means the chip only produces ~30Hz and reading faster just re-fetches the same measurement; offset 4 avoids colliding with mag at 0 or baro at 2).

nodes.label: Two I2C timeouts — 50ms init, 8ms runtime
nodes.rationale: INIT uses 50ms because it runs once at boot with nobody waiting, and generous timing prevents a slow-starting chip (100ms reset, PLL settle) from being wrongly declared absent. RUNTIME uses 8ms because it runs 250 times a second and every millisecond waited is a millisecond the flight loop has no new sample; a 14-byte transaction at 400kHz takes ~0.4ms, so 8ms is 20x margin. Keeping 50ms at runtime would let one bus glitch stall the hub for 12 consecutive control periods versus 2, and delays mark_err so staleness surfaces 50ms late. This is NOT retry logic: timeout returns an error, the hub marks it, and the next cycle simply reads again; a truly dead bus trips consecutive_errors and healthy=false on the existing path. Each driver holds an s_io_timeout_ms initialized at the INIT value and lowered to RUNTIME at the END of *_driver_init() — ToF keeps 50ms for i2c_master_probe() and address change, which are init-only.

nodes.label: Bus lease — sensor_hub_suspend / resume for bench commands
nodes.rationale: mag_selftest and calib_baro_ground talk to chips directly so they must borrow the bus. If the lease cannot be acquired the command is CANCELLED rather than run anyway — two parties reading/writing the chip yields a wrong ground-pressure reference that still reports success. While suspended the snapshot keeps its last sample but its timestamp is NOT refreshed, so consumers correctly observe staleness. The ~1s block is only safe because both commands run while DISARMED / at ARM with motors stopped, which is exactly why baro calibration must not be placed after TKO_PRIME/TKO_CLIMB.

nodes.label: Three-tier hardware diagnostics (i2c_scan, imu_int_test, tof_test)
nodes.rationale: Three commands answering three different questions, and running them out of order makes the later ones meaningless. i2c_scan must go first because a driver init failure has exactly three causes — chip unpowered, chip miswired, chip at an unexpected address — and all three look identical in the driver log; the scan borrows the bus and REFUSES to scan rather than scanning over the hub, since an overlapping scan produces false NACKs that readers trust as 'chip absent', worse than no result. imu_int_test exists because the imu_int_active flag only proves INT_ENABLE was written and the ISR installed; it stays 1 even with a severed INT wire until 25 consecutive timeouts. The real question is RATE, measurable only from two imu_int_isr_count samples apart in time, catching ~1000Hz instead of 250Hz (SMPLRT_DIV never reached the chip, so PID runs with dt off by 4x) and erratic counts (floating INT pin producing spurious edges). tof_test deliberately reads from the snapshot rather than I2C directly so it exercises the exact path the control loop uses (driver -> hub -> snapshot); this is where a real failure hid once — driver init OK but the hub never actually read ToF, which a direct I2C read would have reported as 'fine'.

nodes.label: Kill latch + armed gate — two independent layers
nodes.rationale: The latch stops things at the logic layer (early tick exit) and the armed gate at the driver layer (duty forced to 0). CMD_KILL bypasses the command queue entirely because depth 8 can fill and a stop command must never be dropped for 'queue busy'. The latch engages on CMD_KILL, CMD_DISARM, tilt beyond MAX_SAFE_TILT_DEG while airborne, attitude invalid while airborne, and an EMERGENCY resolved as uncontrollable; it never clears on a timer or when the fault goes away — only an explicit CMD_ARM lowers it. CMD_TEST_MOTOR, the only remaining path calling motor_driver_arm() outside the flight sequence, is also refused while latched.

nodes.label: Cross-core KILL race fixed with portMUX_TYPE
nodes.rationale: KILL executes in the caller's context (net/console on CORE 0) while motor_driver_set_duties() runs in stabilize_task on CORE 1, genuinely in parallel. Without a lock this interleaving is legal: core 1 reads s_armed=true and writes CH0=400; core 0 runs all_off() writing CH0..CH3=0 and setting s_armed=false; core 1 then writes CH1..CH3=400, OVERWRITING the kill. Every flag says 'cut' while three motors keep spinning until the next write — indefinitely if stabilize_task hangs right after. The kill latch cannot help because it only blocks the NEXT tick and the current one is already past its check. The fix puts 'read armed gate + write 4 channels' inside ONE portMUX_TYPE critical section (a multi-core spinlock, unlike a FreeRTOS mutex which only arbitrates tasks); both remaining orderings end with motors off. The section contains only four LEDC register writes (~few us) and nothing blocking, which is mandatory since portENTER_CRITICAL disables interrupts on the current core. A mutex is deliberately not used: the KILL path must work even if the task holding a lock is hung.

nodes.label: Tick with no new IMU sample — what runs, what is skipped
nodes.rationale: imu_updated = (imu_h.seq changed) && (sample age <= SENSOR_IMU_STALE_US) is the deciding flag, and neither imu.ok nor imu_fresh can replace it: imu.ok=false blocks nothing because mahony_update() takes gyro/accel directly and the old values are still sitting in the snapshot; imu_fresh alone would allow 5 consecutive ticks (20ms/4ms) to re-integrate the same sample since it stays 'not yet expired' the whole window. Skipped on a stale tick: mahony_update, alt_estimator_update, gyro/accel calibration accumulation. Still run: deadline monitor, kill latch, SP watchdog, tilt/attitude-stale failsafe, Commander, FSM, mixer and motor write. The attitude I-term FREEZES rather than resetting. P/D keep running because they are PURE FUNCTIONS of current state — re-running them on the same data yields the same command, harmlessly holding stabilizing moment — whereas I ACCUMULATES, so each repeated tick loads the same error again and 5 lost ticks means I is charged 5x reality, unloading as a torque jolt exactly when samples return. Past SENSOR_IMU_STALE_US (20ms) Commander trips a HARD fault 'imu stale'.

nodes.label: fusion_dt — integration uses sample-to-sample time, not tick-to-tick
nodes.rationale: dt for integration is the time between two SAMPLES (accumulated across skipped ticks), not between two ticks. Losing 3 samples and then integrating with one tick's dt under-counts angle/velocity by exactly the lost interval. Clamped to [CONTROL_DT_MIN_S, CONTROL_DT_MAX_S]. Relatedly, dt in the loop is MEASURED, never the constant 1/250 — running off-cadence with a constant scales every PID/estimator coefficient wrong, silently and with no error reported.

nodes.label: ulTaskNotifyTake(pdTRUE) — no catch-up on backlog
nodes.rationale: Clearing the count on take means a delayed task discards the backlog and processes only the NEWEST sample, never replaying. For a control loop that is correct: stale data has no value. The hub calls xTaskNotifyGive UNCONDITIONALLY every cycle even when the IMU read failed, because it is the flight loop's clock and the loop MUST run for safety/failsafe/Commander to run; a failed sample does not bump seq (mark_err) so the loop still distinguishes them. The notify wait's timeout has a floor of 1 tick, since a timeout of 0 would turn it into a 100% CPU busy-loop.

nodes.label: Telemetry is strictly one-way outbound
nodes.rationale: stabilize_task never reads s_telemetry back as flight-logic input; internal state is s_prearm/s_tko_state/s_alt_est. Reading telemetry back means changing its format or filtering would accidentally change flight behaviour — which is exactly what happened before, when the arm guard read s_telemetry and prettifying the graph output altered flight logic. Likewise every command source (console USB, UDP ground station, MicroPython fc.*) shares ONE queue via flight_core_push_command(), so no path bypasses FSM + Commander.

nodes.label: Commander evaluates in every armed state
nodes.rationale: commander_evaluate() used to be called only in HOLDING/FLYING, so losing heartbeat during TAKING_OFF, battery sagging during LANDING, or the IMU dying while ARMED went entirely undetected. It now runs in all states and filters internally on cin.state; the caller no longer filters on its behalf, since that helpful filtering was itself the hole. imu_stale is deliberately separate from imu_ok because Mahony still reports 'valid' while chewing an old sample — a far more dangerous case since everything LOOKS normal while attitude sits frozen and the real drone tilts away. The three 'ignore' entries under LANDING are intentional: already descending, re-entering LANDING would only reset the descent phase in progress.

nodes.label: ARM gate — ordered prearm_check() and arm_reject_t reporting
nodes.rationale: 18 ordered conditions, stopping at the FIRST failure and recording it in arm_reject_t (wired out as ARMREJ=/ARMRSEQ=). The STATE branch used to be COMPLETELY SILENT — only an ESP_LOGW visible on the USB console, while console/GUI over UDP got back an 'ARMED' guess inferred from the attitude guard even when the command had just been rejected; ARMREJ/ARMRSEQ exist because of that hole, with _seq incrementing only on genuine rejections so the GUI can tell 'same old reason' from 'just retried and failed again'. Reject #18 (HOVER_LATCH_VOLT_LOW, <3.4V) must not be merged with #9 (BATTERY_LOW): #9 is Commander's safety floor while 3.4V is the hover model's validity boundary — below it the model extrapolates past the collective ceiling (900*(4.2/3.2)^2.6 = 1825 > 1700) and gets clamped BELOW true hover, falling back into the exact 'drone sits inert' hole the latch was built to fill. Mag calibration was demoted from an ARM requirement to optional; only gyro and accel remain mandatory.

nodes.label: ARM anchors baro ground and ToF ground-ref (moved out of TAKEOFF)
nodes.rationale: Order inside CMD_ARM is deliberate: prearm_check() runs FIRST using the OLD reference, then hover_ff/prime_duty latch, then baro_driver_calibrate_ground(), alt_estimator_reanchor(), and alt_estimator_set_tof_ground_ref() from the hub snapshot (no direct I2C). Reversing it (calibrate first) would make reanchor() set valid=false so prearm_check() then fails on 'estimator invalid', blocking its own ARM. The hover latch sits BEFORE baro calibration because ~940ms of blocking plus reanchor() follow it — failing after that would mean the estimator's 0m reference had already been changed before ARM was abandoned, leaving the system half-configured with nobody having asked for it. A failed calibration REFUSES ARM outright rather than transitioning, since alt_estimator treats baro as its anchor and a wrong reference corrupts everything downstream. Because the reference is fixed at ARM, CMD_TAKEOFF no longer recalibrates: TAKEOFF responds instantly and reanchor() can no longer set valid=false right as TKO_PRIME begins. FSM_ARMED is excluded from Commander's 'estimator lost' check precisely because of the one-tick invalid window.

nodes.label: CMD_TAKEOFF gate — takeoff_reject_t (separate from prearm_check)
nodes.rationale: STATE / NO_CORRECTION / ALT_EST_INVALID, published as TKOREJ=/TKORSEQ= and re-registered as NONE on each attempt. NO_CORRECTION requires at least ONE source (baro OR ToF) rather than hard-coding baro: the previous 'if (!baro_ok) reject' meant disabling baro made takeoff impossible even with a perfectly working ToF. command_parser.c replies only 'sent', never 'started', because it can only observe FSM state from outside while NO_CORRECTION/ALT_EST_INVALID are known solely to flight_core.c — duplicating the condition in two places is the surest way to make them diverge; the real outcome arrives in the next STATUS line's TKOREJ=. All three CMD_TAKEOFF paths (@ALT TAKEOFF, @ALT MODE 3, key 't') now check flight_core_push_command()'s return value, because ignoring it meant a full queue silently vanished the command while the GUI reported 'sent'.

nodes.label: TAKEOFF sequence — PRIME / CLIMB / HOLD with slew-rate-limited target
nodes.rationale: One control loop runs throughout: target_z slews (rate-limited) -> Z-PID -> vz_target -> Vz-PID (hover_ff + P + I) -> throttle. No 'ramp to lift', no 'latch hover at handover', no switching throttle sources. Three anti-windup properties, each load-bearing: (1) target_z starts at CURRENT ALTITUDE (ground_alt_m measured at the PRIME->CLIMB edge), so first-tick Z error is ~0 — setting target to the destination while still grounded reproduces the naive-PID behaviour that launches the drone the moment it has enough thrust; (2) PRIME runs no Z/Vz PID at all, since letting them run charges I before the drone can lift, destroying property 1; (3) hover_ff is a coarse feedforward latched from battery voltage at ARM, with no second constant for the same physical quantity — two numbers for one thing are guaranteed to diverge and produce a throttle step at handover.

nodes.label: hover_model.h — hover_ff latched from battery voltage at ARM
nodes.rationale: hover(V) = 900 * (4.2/V)^2.6 clamped to [800,1700], fit from two bench measurements (4.2V -> ~900 duty, 3.6V -> ~1350) and cross-checked at 3.6V -> 1344, inside the measured 1300-1400 band. Needed because a compile-time constant cannot be right across the voltage range: flying at 3.6V with hover_ff=1000 leaves a ~350 duty deficit that I must crawl up to cover at dI/dt = Ki*vz_err — the real cause of 'arm and the drone sits inert for ten-plus seconds', which is a feedforward anchored at the wrong point, not a Ki tuning problem. The latch avoids the removed continuous compensation's flaw for two independent reasons: vbat is read ONCE at ARM with motors still stopped (FSM DISARMED, armed gate closed, throttle locked at 0) so it is a NO-LOAD voltage, then frozen with no feedback path from throttle back to hover_ff; and it anchors an ADDITIVE term rather than multiplying the final output. vbat uses the MEDIAN of 5 samples (~500ms at 10Hz ADC), not the instantaneous one — the ADC occasionally emits a wild sample and averaging lets it drag the result: one 1.2V sample among four 3.9V ones shifts the latched hover by 517 duty under a mean. The ring buffer filters by seq so one sample is not counted 25 times at 250Hz. HOVER_LATCH_ENABLED=0 in app_config.h restores the old behaviour exactly.

nodes.label: PRIME_DUTY must be well below hover
nodes.rationale: If the drone lifts DURING prime it is flying on open-loop throttle — precisely what this architecture removed. TAKEOFF_PRIME_DUTY = TAKEOFF_PRIME_HOVER_FRAC (70%) * hover: above the brushed motor dead zone, far below liftoff. This inverts the old design where SPOOL_DUTY >= hover because ramping was the only thing that lifted the drone. TAKEOFF_PRIME_HOVER_FRAC is the SINGLE source of that ratio, shared by the tuning.h initial value and hover_model_prime_duty()'s battery-latched value — retyping 0.70 elsewhere means PRIME throttle silently differs between flights.

nodes.label: No I preload at the PRIME->CLIMB edge
nodes.rationale: The old-style preload (vz_integral = prime_duty - hover_ff) computes 780-1300 = -520, clamped to -300, forcing the Vz loop to crawl back UP for ~5.6s just to regain true hover — longer than TAKEOFF_NO_LIFT_TIMEOUT_MS (3s), so the drone aborts before it can lift. Preload was correct in the old design only because spool_duty == hover made it ~0; here prime_duty is DELIBERATELY far below hover, so preloading discards exactly the feedforward the architecture depends on. The consequence is a deliberate throttle step at this edge (prime_duty -> ~hover_ff): the 'no throttle jolt' constraint applies to CLIMB->HOLD (same controller continuing) and not here, where control switches from open-loop to closed-loop with nothing to keep continuous.

nodes.label: Pure slew rate limiter for target_z (not an exponential trajectory)
nodes.rationale: A pure rate limiter reaches the destination by TRUE EQUALITY, unlike the old vz_sp = kp*(target - z_sp) exponential which never actually equals the target and therefore needed a separate arrival tolerance — a tolerance set too small once aborted a completely correct takeoff on timeout. TAKEOFF_MAX_CLIMB_MS deliberately serves two roles at once (target_z slew speed AND the |vz_target| ceiling out of the Z-PID) and must be the same number: a smaller ceiling lets the target outrun the drone so error grows in the naive-PID way, a larger one is meaningless. Raised 0.15 -> 0.35 m/s to fix a logged defect: throughout CLIMB the altitude PID was COMMANDING DESCENT while the drone climbed, because 0.15 m/s is slower than the natural climb rate at hover_ff throttle, so the target crawled 3-4x behind the drone (ALTm +0.13m vs ZSP +0.03m), ZERR went negative, VZTGT commanded down and VZI charged negative continuously. The PID was not wrong — it was braking as instructed — but it was fighting its own feedforward and losing.

nodes.label: Pre-liftoff |I| is LIMITED, not frozen
nodes.rationale: Slew makes the error SMALL, not ZERO, so a drone held down (snagged prop, overload) still sees target_z climbing and accumulates one-directional error — I would grow until TIMEOUT fires at 3s. TAKEOFF_PRELIFT_I_LIMIT_DUTY caps that growth without freezing, because an early revision of this same refactor DID freeze it and measured two consequences: the drone lost the authority to find its lift point when true hover exceeded the estimate, and since the ceiling was never reached the 'cannot lift' fault was misreported as TIMEOUT instead of its actual cause.

nodes.label: TKO_ABORT — all reasons route through EMERGENCY
nodes.rationale: TIMEOUT (no lift within 3s, or 15s total), TOF_LOST (altitude source lost 300ms continuously, counted only from CLIMB since PRIME does not rely on the estimator), and TILT (>45deg sustained 60ms, the window preventing one bad Mahony sample from killing a normal flight). Unlike the old design where the module itself chose ARMED vs LANDING based on liftoff_confirmed, every abort now calls fsm_on_hard_fault() -> EMERGENCY and lets EMERGENCY resolve in the SAME tick via fsm_on_emergency_resolve(controllable). The takeoff sequence does not need to know that policy, which avoids two parallel policy implementations drifting apart. During the TOF_LOST grace window the cascade does not run on garbage est_z — st->last_throttle is held.

nodes.label: CLIMB -> HOLD handover is seamless
nodes.rationale: Entered when target_z == final_target_m by true equality AND |est_z - final_target| <= TAKEOFF_HOLD_ENTER_TOL_M (0.05m) sustained for TAKEOFF_HOLD_ENTER_MS (300ms) — the sustain window substitutes for a separate |vz| check, since a drone overshooting cannot stay inside the tolerance for the whole window. No preload, no reset, no throttle change: hold_st is already engaged with vz_integral holding the LEARNED true hover, and alt_hold_run() continues from that exact state on the same cascade with a stationary target, so no throttle step occurs. s_alt_target_m is set to final_target_m — the COMMANDED target, not the noisy current Z.

nodes.label: Test D — records a known gap, not a protection
nodes.rationale: CLIMB->HOLD handover is now purely time-based, and target_z is a pure rate limiter, so it advances IDENTICALLY whether or not the drone is actually flying. The mathematical consequence: any fault detector slower than the handover instant can never fire during TAKING_OFF. For a 0.5m target, handover lands at ~5.8s while I reaches its limit at ~50s — so a physically blocked drone is still handed to HOLDING while sitting on the ground. TKO_ABORT_STUCK (TKOAB=5, based on vz_integral >= 0.95*i_limit or collective at ceiling) exists and is correct but simply cannot fire inside that window. The current real defence is telemetry — sustained ALTSAT=1 plus TKOI pinned at its limit plus flat ALTm means manual KILL. Closing it properly requires moving detection into HOLDING, with Commander treating sustained alt-PID saturation as a soft fault -> LANDING.

nodes.label: R1/R2 source-reading regression tests
nodes.rationale: Two review questions had to be answerable before trusting the rewrite: does target_z really start at current altitude, and does PRIME really not run the Z/Vz PID. python/test_takeoff_flow_offline.py section (R) reads the SOURCE rather than runtime behaviour to lock both: target_z_m = ground_alt_m (not hard-coded 0, not assigned final_target_m at startup), and the file's single alt_hold_vz_cascade() call must appear AFTER the `if (phase == TKO_PRIME)` block that returns.

nodes.label: command_queue (FreeRTOS, depth 8)
nodes.rationale: Multi-writer, single-reader. Non-blocking xQueueSend so a full queue returns false immediately rather than stalling the caller; CMD_KILL deliberately bypasses it because a stop command must not be lost to a busy queue.

nodes.label: sensor_snapshot_t (value + seq + timestamp + valid + healthy)
nodes.rationale: Mutex-guarded with one writer (the hub). Step 1 of every tick is a memcpy of this snapshot, never an I2C read, and 'new sample' is determined by seq rather than the ok flag.

nodes.label: src/main.c — second command entry point (console USB + UDP)
nodes.rationale: Parallel to the MicroPython tier, used when building without MicroPython or to let a PC GUI (tools/uav_udp_console.py) control and tune directly. It calls exactly the same two public APIs as fc_bridge.c (flight_core_push_command / flight_core_read_telemetry) — there is no shortcut path into flight_core.

nodes.label: fc_module.c / fc_bridge.c are marshal-only
nodes.rationale: They only marshal data and contain no `if` related to flight logic. fc_api.py is the ONLY place blocking semantics (poll + timeout) are added; the C module fc.* pushes a command and returns immediately. fc_bridge_init() is also the single place that reads main/board_config.h to build flight_core_board_config_t for flight_core_start().

nodes.label: Firmware-owned takeoff completion (alt_mm carried in command_t)
nodes.rationale: fc.takeoff(800) is now the ONLY command needed: the target lives inside command_t and the firmware runs PRIME->CLIMB->HOLD to exactly 800mm before handing over to HOLDING, so fc_api.takeoff() only polls. Previously alt_mm was ignored — firmware spooled, lifted, latched the target at whatever altitude it reached (~20cm), and fc_api had to send a SECOND set_altitude(800) after seeing HOLDING. A script crash or lost link between the two commands left the drone hovering just off the ground with nobody to complete or cancel it. That was flight semantics leaking up into the Python tier; the firmware now owns completing-or-safely-aborting even if MicroPython disappears entirely.

nodes.label: LANDING sequence - multi-condition touchdown
nodes.rationale: State chain DESCEND -> FLARE -> CONTACT_CANDIDATE -> TOUCHDOWN, with a BLIND branch when Z-est is lost too long (BLIND returns to DESCEND if Z-est recovers, or reaches TOUCHDOWN when throttle falls below the floor). TOUCHDOWN ramps throttle to 0 then DISARMED. landing_run() receives land_height_m and land_tof_agl_m from alt_estimator_agl_m() / alt_estimator_tof_agl_m().

nodes.label: LANDING runs on CLEARANCE, never absolute Z
nodes.rationale: Pressing land while flying over a table must descend to the TABLE SURFACE, not to floor altitude - targeting floor altitude means flying into the table. Both inputs come from the RAW tof_vertical_m (section 4.6), so they stay correct even when terrain_off_m has gone stale. Ignoring this is a MEASURED defect: a stale TOFF of 0.693 against a true clearance of 0.019m made landing believe it had 70cm left to descend, so touchdown never triggered and the motors kept running.

nodes.label: CONTACT_CANDIDATE - 4-evidence touchdown debounce
nodes.rationale: World Z comes from the accel-primary estimator and near the ground it is noisy by +-0.3-1m, many times larger than touchdown_alt_m (0.05m). Having a ToF does NOT remove the problem: close to the ground is exactly where propwash and ground effect are worst, and ToF is additionally gated when it is not looking at the locked floor surface. The old code cut motors the moment alt < touchdown_alt_m, so a single pressure dip from wind or propwash was enough to CUT MOTORS IN MID-AIR - the most reliably drone-killing bug in the file. Four pieces of evidence are scored: throttle down near the landing floor; small |Vz| DESPITE commanding descent; low Z (weakest, cannot decide alone); and Z having STOPPED DECREASING while still commanding descent (the strongest sign - mechanically blocked). Requires >=3/4 held ~300ms. Inside CONTACT_CANDIDATE the drone stays FULLY controlled and merely descends at the slowest rate, so a false positive simply returns to normal descent leaving no trace.

nodes.label: Three altitude quantities plus clearance - do not mix them
nodes.rationale: tof_vertical_m is the RAW measurement (already cos(tilt)-compensated), the distance to the surface immediately below; it passes through neither terrain_off nor fusion. terrain_off_m is the height of that surface relative to the TAKEOFF FLOOR. alt_m is ABSOLUTE altitude above the floor = raw_agl + terrain_off_m, and it is what the altitude PID consumes. agl_m() is the CLEARANCE beneath the belly and prefers raw tof_vertical_m; it is what the collision guard and landing touchdown consume. On the takeoff floor terrain_off_m = 0; on a 0.75m table it is 0.75. Committing an offset exactly equal to the step keeps alt_m CONTINUOUS across the jump so the PID sees nothing unusual.

nodes.label: agl_m() must come from the raw measurement, not alt_m - terrain_off_m
nodes.rationale: The old formula agl = alt_m - terrain_off_m is algebraically tempting but wrong, because alt_m ALREADY CONTAINS terrain_off_m. When the offset is wrong both terms carry the SAME error, so it does not cancel - it propagates straight into clearance. Measured on a flight onto a table: stale TOFF 0.693, true clearance (TOFV) 0.019m (about to touch), old-formula agl 0.712m. Landing believed it had 70cm left while the drone was already against the table surface, so touchdown never fired and the motors ran on. The new version prefers raw tof_vertical_m, which does not depend on terrain_off and stays correct even when the offset is completely wrong; it falls back to alt_m - terrain_off_m only when the raw measurement is outside geometric range (absorbing surface, too far), where it is the best remaining estimate.

nodes.label: Terrain offset - flying over furniture without losing reference
nodes.rationale: Compile-time TERRAIN_OFFSET_ENABLED in app_config.h; disabled reproduces the old behaviour exactly with terrain_off_m pinned at 0. Detection uses a RESIDUAL rather than a raw threshold: d_range = tof_vertical_m - prev; expected = vz_accel_only_ms * tof_dt_s; residual = d_range - expected. Crossing TERR_JUMP_THRESH_M opens a pending candidate; TERR_CONFIRM_N = 3 consecutive samples matching within TERR_CONFIRM_TOL_M commit it. FRAME telemetry distinguishes DATUM (hold height above the floor) from AGL (follow terrain).

nodes.label: Terrain residual expected term must use vz_accel_only_ms
nodes.rationale: vz_ms has already been corrected by ToF (see the fuse block at the end of alt_estimator_update), so using it makes the detector a CLOSED FEEDBACK LOOP: the range jump pumps into vz_ms, expected swells in the same direction as the jump, the residual is partly cancelled, and a real terrain step can drop below threshold and NEVER BE DETECTED. vz_accel_only_ms integrates purely from az_corrected_ms2 and never takes a ToF correction.

nodes.label: Candidate offset must ACCUMULATE, not be latched once
nodes.rationale: A terrain step does NOT arrive in a single sample. Flight log climbing onto a table: TOFV 0.890 -> 0.338 -> 0.126 -> 0.119 -> 0.110 while alt_m coasted ~0.86, with TRES -0.552 on the first sample then smaller negatives. The old code latched the candidate once on the first sample (terr_cand_offset_m = terrain_off_m - residual) and froze it; the range then slid a further ~0.23m, so the candidate was immediately obsolete - cand_z came out 0.678/0.671/0.662 against alt_m 0.86, i.e. off by 0.182/0.189/0.198m. That exceeds TERR_CONFIRM_TOL_M (0.10) so confirm_cnt reset EVERY sample, TERR_CONFIRM_N was never reached, TERR_PENDING_TIMEOUT_MS expired, correction was lost, and a soft fault forced LANDING mid-flight. The fix adds each still-over-threshold sample's share (terr_cand_offset_m -= residual) so that once the step is fully traversed the residual returns to ~0, the candidate stops moving, cand_z matches alt_m and it commits. Replayed against that same logged data (python/test_terrain_accumulate_offline.py): old = no commit -> LANDING; new = COMMIT TOFF +0.764 after 120ms. False positives are not a risk because accumulation only happens for samples already past TERR_JUMP_THRESH_M, which ordinary ToF noise (+-1-3cm) never crosses - the test locks all three noise levels.

nodes.label: Terrain commit sanity check (B3)
nodes.rationale: |cand - current| <= TERR_MAX_STEP_M (1.5m). Exceeding it means a bad measurement (garbage sample, mirror reflection, out of range), so the commit is REFUSED, the old offset is kept, and TREJ increments. This also bounds an implausible accumulated total.

nodes.label: Timeout counted by CLOCK vs commit counted by SAMPLES
nodes.rationale: The confirm/commit path lives inside if (tof_new) and therefore runs at the 25Hz ToF rate - about 6-7 times in 260ms - while the pending-timeout check runs on the 250Hz control tick, about 65 times in the same window. The two cadences differ by an order of magnitude. In the logged flight the candidate HAD already met the commit criterion (cand_z 1.144 vs alt_m 1.09, off by 0.054 < TERR_CONFIRM_TOL_M 0.10), but detection needed 2 samples plus 3 to confirm = 200ms, leaving only 60ms of margin - and TOFAGE was jumping 7->45ms, so slipping one sample blew the deadline. The fix adds terr_samples_seen and requires BOTH conditions: terr_samples_seen >= TERR_MIN_SAMPLES_BEFORE_TIMEOUT (= TERR_CONFIRM_N + 1, exactly the theoretical sample count needed) AND the elapsed time. This does not relax the criterion, it only guarantees confirm gets a fair chance to run. If ToF dies outright the counter simply stops and the independent degraded path (300ms) still lands normally, so this flag cannot hang the system.

nodes.label: terr_offset_stale - timeout must fail SAFE
nodes.rationale: The old code, on timeout, discarded only that one suspicion and immediately let ToF fuse again using the OLD terrain_off_m - which is precisely what produced a false 0.5m jump (raw 1.01 + stale TOFF 0.693 = 1.70 against alt_m coasting at 1.09, an innovation of +0.61m) that faulted the estimator and landed the drone mid-flight. The deeper reason: a timeout means 'we KNOW the surface changed but we do NOT know by how much', and a stale offset in that situation is GARBAGE, not a safe interim value. The fix sets terr_offset_stale = true on timeout, and the tof_fusable block then forces tof_fusable = false with tof_surface_state = OTHER, so ToF stops correcting ABSOLUTE Z while the estimator coasts on the IMU bridge and degraded handles a CONTROLLED descent instead of losing control to a phantom jump. Raw range remains usable throughout because agl_m() reads tof_vertical_m directly, so the collision guard and landing touchdown still have real measurements - only absolute Z is untrusted. The flag is cleared in exactly three places (successful commit, terrain_rebase(), and reset via lock_floor_at / prepare_takeoff); failing to clear it would lock ToF out permanently after a single timeout.

nodes.label: terr_pending deadlock - the bug that disabled this feature
nodes.rationale: Measured on hardware: TOFF=-0.315 TPEND=1 TCMT=1 TOFFUSE=0 TOFTRACK=0, with TOFR climbing steadily while TOFA sat frozen at 177-178. The cycle: terr_pending = true forces tof_fusable = false (correct by design - do not consume a range you currently distrust), but tof_fusable = false means no sample reaches the confirm branch, so terr_confirm_cnt neither increments nor resets and terr_pending is STUCK AT 1 FOREVER, correction is lost, and a soft fault lands the drone mid-flight. Three conditions must hold SIMULTANEOUSLY or the bug returns: (1) TERR_PENDING_TIMEOUT_MS = 260 must CANCEL the suspicion rather than commit it, since committing an unconfirmed candidate writes a possibly-wrong offset into DURABLE state - exactly what produced TOFF=-0.315 and then rejected every subsequent sample; (2) the timeout must be SHORTER than ALT_EST_NO_CORRECTION_DEGRADED_MS (300ms), guarded by _Static_assert - the first patch mistakenly compared against ALT_EST_TOF_LOST_MS, and without also making degraded time-based the fault fires on the very first tick making the timeout useless; 260ms is not arbitrary but clamped from both sides by the 40ms ToF cadence, floor (N+1)*40 = 160ms and ceiling 300 - 40 = 260ms, with the old N=4/200ms configuration having exactly ZERO margin; (3) the escape block must sit OUTSIDE if (tof_new), since inside it would only run when a new sample arrives - the very condition it exists to fix.

nodes.label: Minimum clearance guard (B8) - the last safety net
nodes.rationale: Runs AFTER every throttle path including W/S because it must BEAT all of them: however wrong the offset logic goes, and even while the pilot holds S, the drone must not be driven into the table. Condition: (hold_driving || flying_no_alt_pid) && tof_fusable && agl_now_m < TERR_MIN_CLEARANCE_M (0.25m) -> force vz_target = max(current command, TERR_ESCAPE_VZ_MS 0.20 m/s), rebasing terrain_off_m on the guard's rising edge. Testing flying_no_alt_pid is MANDATORY: FLYING deliberately sets hold_driving=false, so checking hold_driving alone would disable the guard throughout FLYING - exactly when it is most needed, flying laterally toward an obstacle.

nodes.label: Throttle rise-rate cap must accumulate the fraction
nodes.rationale: THROTTLE_MAX_RISE_DUTY_PER_S = 500 exists because hovering at ~23cm (below the 25cm guard) trips the guard EVERY tick and every tick overwrites the latch: THR 995 -> 995 -> 1095 -> 1995 -> 2000, i.e. +900 duty in one 5ms tick. But the cap must accumulate the fractional remainder rather than truncating with (int): 500 * 0.004s = 2.0 duty/tick is fine, yet at 150 duty/s (int)(150*0.004) = 0 so rise_cap = latch and throttle can NEVER increase - completely disabling the anti-collision guard. A rate limiter silently turns into a hard lock.

nodes.label: FSM_FLYING - outer cascade stage off, inner stage kept
nodes.rationale: The altitude cascade has two stages; entering FLYING disables only the outer one (alt -> vz_target) while the inner stage (vz -> throttle) keeps running with vz_target = 0. The outer stage must go because ToF measures distance to the surface immediately below: crossing a 0.75m table at 1.2m altitude makes range jump 1.2 -> 0.45, which the outer stage reads as 'dropped 0.75m' and answers with a vertical throttle surge. The inner stage is kept because it reads vz, not range - and vz taken from pure accel has NO IDEA a table is underneath, so it stays correct straight through the jump.

nodes.label: Disabling BOTH cascade stages was a real hole
nodes.rationale: The previous version disabled both stages, freezing throttle at s_flying_throttle_latch. 'Throttle held constant' does NOT mean 'altitude held constant': if the drone entered FLYING with vz != 0 (just released W/S, just escaped the guard, or merely propwash) it then DRIFTED FREELY for the whole FLYING segment. A micro quad can lose 10-20cm in 300ms, and FLYING_TO_HOLD_SETTLE_MS is exactly 300ms.

nodes.label: FLYING vz source must be accel-only
nodes.rationale: FLYING_VZ_USE_ACCEL_ONLY selects vz_accel_only_ms over vz_ms. alt_estimator fuses ToF into vz_ms through TWO paths: dv = ALT_EST_TOF_VZ_GAIN * (tof_vz_lpf_ms - vz_ms), plus a clamped ALT_EST_TOF_INNOV_VZ_GAIN * iz / tof_dt_s term. Crossing a table makes iz jump 0.75m, so the second path injects a PHANTOM VELOCITY into vz_ms - clamped to 0.20 m/s but still wrong-signed and persisting for many ticks. Having the Vz loop react to that fake number is WORSE than disabling it outright.

nodes.label: Bumpless I load on the FIRST tick only
nodes.rationale: On entering FLYING, vz_integral is seeded from clampf(latch - hover, +-FLYING_VZ_ILIMIT_DUTY) exactly once. The s_flying_vz_engaged flag MUST be separate from (s_flying_throttle_latch < 0): the latch is now rewritten EVERY tick as it chases the cascade output, so it can no longer serve as a 'first tick' marker - sharing one flag would reload I every tick, continuously overwriting it and stripping the Vz loop of its integral term entirely. FLYING_VZ_ILIMIT_DUTY = 120 is tighter than ALT_HOLD_VZ_ILIMIT = 500 because in FLYING the drone banks to translate so slightly negative vz is NORMAL rather than an error to integrate away; letting I range as wide as in HOLDING would carry a bias lump into the stick release and cause a climb.

nodes.label: FLYING -> HOLDING handover is already bumpless
nodes.rationale: The FLYING exit block deliberately does NOT touch s_hold_state.vz_integral. The Vz loop in FLYING has been running on that very variable, so it already holds exactly the throttle needed for vz = 0; alt_hold_run() on the next tick sees st->engaged == true and therefore skips alt_hold_preload(), continuing from that value. That is the definition of bumpless. Resetting I to 0 here would drop throttle by roughly a full hover on HOLDING's first tick, sinking the drone at the moment the stick is released.

nodes.label: W/S in FLYING is a TEMPORARY offset, and ordering is part of the contract
nodes.rationale: Contract: hold the key -> throttle = base + WS_THROTTLE_OFFSET_DUTY (150); release -> base. The offset must be added AFTER s_flying_throttle_latch has been written from the cascade output. Adding it BEFORE makes the next tick treat the offset-inclusive throttle as the new base and add again - the measured accumulation bug: THR 999 -> 999 -> 1799 -> 2000 -> 2000 with MHR=0 at the ceiling, THRCORR -1 -> -1 -> 799 -> 1000 -> 1000. The GUI sends a keepalive every 100ms while a key is held (mandatory, since the firmware has a BENCH_OFFSET_STALE_US watchdog), so each packet added once more: five packets = +500, pinned at the ceiling and STAYING there after release because the latch is durable state. The principle: a keepalive is a mechanism to KEEP A COMMAND ALIVE, not a NEW command - reading it as new counts repetitions of one intention. The Vz loop deliberately FIGHTS this offset: hold W -> drone climbs -> vz > 0 -> the cascade lowers I to pull back to vz = 0; release and the base is now slightly lower so the drone settles at a NEW altitude. That is the desired behaviour - W/S changes ALTITUDE, not permanently a throttle number. Freezing I while the key is held would return the drone to its old altitude on release, making W/S do nothing at all.

nodes.label: BENCH_MODE - full logic, no motor output
nodes.rationale: BENCH_MODE_ENABLED (app_config.h), default 0. Everything runs exactly as in a real flight - estimator, both cascade stages, attitude PID, mixer, FSM, failsafe, telemetry - with one difference: the final LEDC write always writes 0, so the four motors never spin. It exists to tune and read logs on the desk without removing propellers, watching THR/VZI/TOFF/TTMO react to an object passed under the ToF with no risk of the drone jumping.

nodes.label: BENCH_MODE blocks at the lowest layer, and still writes 0
nodes.rationale: The block lives in motor_driver_set_duties() alongside the hardware armed gate, inside the same portENTER_CRITICAL region (armed = s_armed && !bench_block). It is deliberately NOT placed in flight_core.c, which has THREE call sites for motor_driver_set_duties() - adding a fourth guarantees somebody eventually forgets one. Blocking at the driver leaves no path around it. It still WRITES 0 to LEDC rather than returning early, for the same reason as the armed gate: LEDC registers hold their value, so an early return would leave the motors spinning at the previously written duty. When enabled the firmware prints a FIVE-LINE warning at boot, because leaving this flag at 1 by accident means the motors never spin and the user goes hunting for a hardware fault.

nodes.label: fc_features.h compile-time feature flags
nodes.rationale: FC_FEATURE_MAG/BARO/TOF/BATTERY/HOVER_LATCH/TERRAIN_OFFSET/FLOOR_GATE/BENCH_MODE, fed from main/app_config.h. A flag at 0 means the driver or feature is NOT COMPILED IN at all, so calling it mistakenly is a compile error rather than a runtime surprise. BENCH_MODE defaults to 0 unlike the sensor flags which default to 1, precisely so that 'app_config.h not found' means REAL FLIGHT.

nodes.label: STATUS line format and STATUS_RE parsing contract
nodes.rationale: Emitted by src/telemetry_format.c and consumed by tools/uav_udp_console.py. The GUI shows fields ONLY WHEN THERE IS A PROBLEM, because a status line that always displays everything trains the reader to ignore all of it. python/test_status_parse_offline.py locks the exact group count of STATUS_RE and each field index: inserting a field mid-line without updating indices shifts the GUI's reading of the ENTIRE tail, which is exactly what that test exists to catch. Every tail block is optional so a new GUI still parses old firmware and vice versa; the terrain fields sit past HOVLD at TELEMETRY_LEVEL >= 2 where STATUS_RE swallows the remainder, so adding or removing them there does not break the regex.

nodes.label: Terrain telemetry fields (TOFF, TPEND, TCMT, TREJ, TTMO, TRES, TSTALE, TCAND, TCNT, TSEEN, CLR, FRAME)
nodes.rationale: TOFF = terrain_off_m, the height of the surface currently viewed relative to the takeoff floor. TPEND = a step is SUSPECTED but unconfirmed. TCMT = number of offset COMMITS (steps traversed). TREJ = commits REFUSED by the TERR_MAX_STEP_M sanity check. TTMO = suspicions CANCELLED by TERR_PENDING_TIMEOUT_MS. TRES = latest residual in metres, the number used to tune TERR_JUMP_THRESH_M. TSTALE = 1 means the terrain offset is NO LONGER TRUSTED after a transition timeout, ToF has stopped correcting absolute Z, and the estimator is coasting on the IMU bridge. TCAND = the CANDIDATE offset awaiting confirmation, distinct from TOFF which is the accepted one. TCNT = consecutive samples matching the candidate (0..TERR_CONFIRM_N). TSEEN = ToF samples that have passed through the confirm block since entering pending. CLR = TRUE belly clearance taken from RAW tof_vertical_m and independent of TOFF - the number that decides collision and touchdown, NOT ALT. FRAME = 0 DATUM (hold height above floor) / 1 AGL (follow terrain).

nodes.label: TTMO is the first number to read when debugging terrain
nodes.rationale: Sustained TPEND=1 with TTMO RISING STEADILY means the escape path IS running, so TERR_JUMP_THRESH_M is set too low and ordinary ToF noise is raising false alarms. Sustained TPEND=1 with TTMO FROZEN means the escape path is NOT running - the old deadlock of section 4.6 - so disable TERRAIN_OFFSET_ENABLED and keep investigating. TPEND=1 with TSEEN frozen means ToF is not delivering samples at all so confirm has nothing to run on: inspect TOFAGE/TOFR, this is not a terrain bug. TSTALE=1 means a timeout already happened, ToF no longer corrects Z, the drone is flying on the IMU bridge and will go degraded then land - it is the FIRST number to check when a FAULT appears after passing over an object. TCNT repeatedly snapping back to 0 means the candidate is not settling: either TCAND is still moving or coasting alt_m has drifted past TERR_CONFIRM_TOL_M. Crossing an object with TCMT incrementing by 1 and TOFF matching the object's height is correct operation.

nodes.label: TOFAGE vs TOFALIVE - two different questions
nodes.rationale: TOFAGE is the age of the last VALID sample; TOFALIVE is how long the CHIP itself has failed to measure. TOFAGE rising without bound while TOFALIVE stays small means the chip is ALIVE with nothing to measure (sitting below the ~4cm blind spot, out of range, or an absorbing surface) - NOT a fault, which is exactly why the two fields exist separately. TOFALIVE exceeding ALT_EST_TOF_LOST_MS (300ms) means the chip is genuinely silent (bus broken, sensor dead) -> valid=false -> soft fault, the ONLY soft-fault path. Conflating the two was the old bug: reading 0.000m while sitting on the floor was treated as a broken sensor, so EVERY TAKEOFF COMMAND WAS REFUSED on perfectly good hardware.

nodes.label: TKOI - the most important takeoff telemetry field
nodes.rationale: TKOI is the Vz loop's integral, the part that LEARNS true hover. It starts from 0 at the PRIME->CLIMB edge (no preload) and must converge to a stable value approximately equal to (true hover - hover_ff). Rising then settling is correct. Rising to the ceiling followed by TKOAB=1 or TKOAB=5 means the drone cannot lift (weak battery, snagged prop, overload) or hover_ff is set too low. Strongly negative from the start means somebody preloaded it wrongly - the fixed bug of section 4.2. After the battery hover latch, TKOI must be MUCH SMALLER than before, and that is how the model is validated: a correct hover_ff leaves I with almost nothing to learn. Simulated at 3.6V on the same drone: constant hover_ff 1000 needed +43 duty of I and reached 0.000m (never left the ground), while the latched 1344 needed only +15 duty and reached 0.276m. If HOVLD is far from the true hover you know, the two original fit points need remeasuring rather than tuning around.

nodes.label: Safety and loop-timing telemetry fields
nodes.rationale: KILL (latch closed, motors hard-cut, re-ARM required); IAGE/MAGE/BAGE sample ages where a steady rise means sensor_hub has stopped delivering and points at the I2C bus; HDEG heading_degraded meaning yaw is gyro-only and slowly drifting while roll/pitch remain good (not an IMU fault); LDT/LMX/DLM loop dt, peak and missed-deadline ticks where a rising DLM means PID is computing on a wrong dt; MSAT/MRPY/MHR mixer saturation, blocked axis and headroom where sustained saturation means control authority is exhausted; KI showing the AND of both I-term gates; FAULT giving fault_class_t (1=SOFT, 2=HARD); ARMREJ/ARMRSEQ giving the ARM refusal reason and count.

nodes.label: Correlated telemetry pairs worth reading together
nodes.rationale: IAGE rising WHILE LDT stays around 4000us means the control loop is running normally but computing on DEAD DATA - precisely the case imu_stale (split from imu_ok) exists to catch, because everything still looks fine. Sustained MSAT=1 WITH a small MHR is not noise but genuine lack of authority (battery compensation is gone, so it can no longer be blamed for pushing collective up). TKOACT=1 WITH TKOLIFT=0 is NORMAL - it is the window in which the controller is lifting the drone - and only concerning if it persists, at which point read TKOI. TOFAGE rising past 200ms WHILE TOK=1 means driver init succeeded but sensor_hub stopped delivering samples: run tof_test.

nodes.label: UDP protocol - two character modes
nodes.rationale: command_parser_feed_byte() is a per-byte state machine. Outside line mode each byte is an immediate command (r=ARM, k=KILL, d=DISARM, t=TAKEOFF, l=LAND, p=heartbeat, f/q=enable/disable STATUS streaming, s=status, h/?=help). An '@' enters line mode, accumulating until newline or carriage return then dispatching @PID/@MAH/@SP/@TRIM/@ALT/@THR/@TKO/@LAND/@HOVER/@MOVE/@YAW/@TEST/@CMDR/@CAL.

nodes.label: 'f' is required for STATUS - the silent blindness trap
nodes.rationale: s_telemetry_enabled defaults to false, and until it is set the firmware sends NO STATUS lines at all, leaving the GUI COMPLETELY BLIND: no TKOREJ, no takeoff phase, no ToF health. The symptom is 'I pressed TAKEOFF and nothing happened and I cannot tell why' - the command WAS sent and the firmware DID reply, but nobody was listening. The GUI now sends 'f' automatically on connect and runs a 2s watchdog warning if no STATUS arrives after a TAKEOFF press. Command replies (@CAL, @PID, single-char) always work regardless of this flag; only PERIODIC status is gated.

nodes.label: GUI layout and setpoint keepalive cadence
nodes.rationale: The log pane is fixed to the LEFT half via place(relwidth=0.5) with the notebook on the right, because pack(expand) divides slack according to each widget's requested size and the notebook requests several times the log's width - the log ended up with about a third and shrank further with every new panel. Manual control resends @SP SET every 200ms, which must be shorter than the firmware's SP_STALE_TIMEOUT_US (400ms); the old 1.0s keepalive left the setpoint zeroed 60% of the time. w/s are momentary and the GUI sends the identical @THR OFFSET +-100 in every state, with the firmware interpreting it per state: BENCH_RAMP adds directly to duty, HOLDING adds directly to the duty alt_hold just computed then re-anchors the target to current Z, FLYING adds directly on top of the base throttle held by the Vz loop, and every other state ignores it and forces 0. The meaning is now UNIFORM across states: the value on the wire IS duty - one number, one meaning. Releasing the key returns the offset to 0, with a firmware watchdog (BENCH_OFFSET_STALE_US 400ms) treating a command drought as a key release - placed on the tick loop rather than in the handler, because the thing being guarded against is precisely NO COMMAND ARRIVING. Geofence still applies while the key is held: at the ceiling or floor ws_duty is forced to 0 in the VIOLATING direction only, since escaping the boundary must always remain possible. w/s are only accepted while the Manual tab is active (_manual_active()); on another tab the handler returns immediately with NO feedback, which is not a firmware fault.

nodes.label: W/S as +-duty instead of a velocity command - accepted trade-off
nodes.rationale: W/S was formerly a velocity command of +-ALT_HOLD_WS_VZ_MS and was REMOVED at the user's request. The physical argument for the Vz version remains valid and worth knowing: '+100 duty' is DIMENSIONLESS authority, so the same key produces different climb rates depending on battery (hover ~900 duty at 4.2V versus ~1350 at 3.6V), whereas a Vz command has units - holding w climbs 0.10 m/s at any battery level because the Vz loop's I absorbs the difference. The accepted trade-off of returning to +-duty is that on a low battery the same key climbs noticeably slower. ALT_HOLD_WS_VZ_MS (0.10) REMAINS in tuning.h with a _Static_assert bounding it by ALT_HOLD_VZ_LIMIT_MS, in case the Vz mode returns. Magnitude is WS_THROTTLE_OFFSET_DUTY = 150.

nodes.label: Trim roll/pitch persisted to NVS
nodes.rationale: @TRIM SET <roll> <pitch> -> CMD_SET_TRIM -> clamped to +-TRIM_MAX_DEG (10 deg) -> added to the attitude cascade's target roll/pitch and saved to NVS immediately via calibration_save_trim(), sharing the namespace with gyro/accel/mag.

nodes.label: Two trim bugs fixed (timed commands and RAM-only persistence)
nodes.rationale: First, trim VANISHED during timed commands: the previous version added trim only on the setpoint branch, while the timed branch (CMD_MOVE/CMD_SET_YAW) took s_timed_*_deg directly - so during a two-second 'move forward 30 2' the drone drifted by exactly the offset trim exists to cancel. Trim is NOT a setpoint; it is a constant compensating mechanical/CG offset, so 'which command wins' does not apply to it, and it is now added on BOTH branches. Second, trim lived only in RAM and was lost on every power cycle. A third hazard is AXIS SWAPPING AT THE BOUNDARY: NVS stores the EXTERNAL convention (what @TRIM SET accepts) while the internal variables are swapped (s_trim_pitch_deg = external roll), so the load path must swap IDENTICALLY to CMD_SET_TRIM - forgetting rotates trim by 90 degrees after reboot, the hardest kind of silent bug to trace. python/test_trim_offline.py locks both.

nodes.label: ToF tilt compensation via quaternion rzz
nodes.rationale: ToF measures along the BODY axis, not the vertical, so a banked drone measures a longer slanted path than its true height. alt_estimator.c uses rzz = 1 - 2x^2 - 2y^2, element (3,3) of the rotation matrix, which equals cos(roll)*cos(pitch) exactly - verified numerically to within 1.1e-16 (double precision) and INDEPENDENT OF YAW. rzz is used instead of writing cosf(roll)*cosf(pitch) both to avoid two trig calls in a 250Hz loop and to avoid extracting Euler angles only to recombine them, since the quaternion already carries this component. Beyond ALT_EST_TOF_TILT_MIN_COS = 0.87 (~29.5 deg) the sample is REJECTED rather than compensated, because by then the beam has slid to a genuinely different point on the floor instead of measuring the same point obliquely. tilt_cos is a SEPARATE field written EVERY TICK at 250Hz for throttle compensation; it deliberately does not share tof_tilt_cos, which is written only inside if (tof_new) at the ~25Hz ToF rate and FREEZES ENTIRELY if ToF dies.

nodes.label: Innovation gate and floor-measuring machinery - removed
nodes.rationale: The old design locked the floor surface at TAKEOFF, classified surfaces FLOOR/OTHER and applied a 0.25m innovation gate. All of it was removed because of two MEASURED failures. The innovation gate meant flying over a 0.5m object pushed innovation past threshold -> surface=OTHER -> tof_fusable=false -> after 300ms valid=false -> soft fault -> LANDING, i.e. 'fly over an object' EQUALLED 'land automatically'. The floor measurer (floor_add + Welford) meant sitting close to the floor made the VL53L1X read 0.000m (under its ~4cm blind spot), the driver rejected the samples, the statistics window never closed, tof_ground_ref_valid stayed stuck false and EVERY TAKEOFF COMMAND WAS REFUSED. Now raw_agl = tof_vertical_m with nothing subtracted, and jump protection moved to a SLEW-RATE LIMIT on zt, which makes measurements change SMOOTHLY instead of DISCARDING samples, so it can never lead to 'altitude source lost'. Consequence: alt_m now means 'how far above the surface below', not 'how far above the takeoff point', unless terrain offset is enabled.

nodes.label: valid vs degraded - two different questions
nodes.rationale: valid asks whether the state is still usable and goes false when isfinite fails or the ToF chip is genuinely silent (tof_hw_alive=false) - the ONLY soft-fault path. degraded asks how long there has been NO CORRECTION (ALT_EST_NO_CORRECTION_DEGRADED_MS = ALT_EST_TOF_LOST_MS = 300ms). valid=1 degraded=1 is a LEGITIMATE state: z is still a number but is free-running on accel dead reckoning. degraded MUST be counted by TIME rather than hard-assigned - a real fixed bug. The old BRIDGE branch set e->degraded = true the moment ONE sample was unfusable; the correct version computes since_corr_ms from last_tof_accept_us and compares against the threshold. This matters because commander.c faults on the VERY FIRST TICK it sees degraded, with no debounce, so hard-assigning true meant a SINGLE unusable ToF sample (out of range, absorbing surface, suspected terrain step) equalled LANDING MID-FLIGHT - and 'unusable sample' is NORMAL for ToF. last_tof_accept_us == 0 (never had a correction) still reports degraded immediately, which is genuine ToF death and must be caught, so the safety path is intact.

nodes.label: Three ToF track states (LOST / BRIDGE / TRACKING)
nodes.rationale: Silent chip (!tof_hw_alive) -> LOST, valid=0, degraded=1: bus broken or sensor dead, soft fault. Chip reading with a fusable sample -> TRACKING, valid=1, degraded=0: normal. Chip reading but the sample is unusable -> BRIDGE, valid=1, degraded by time: coasting on the IMU, and NOT a fault. The key distinction is 'chip still reading' versus 'sample usable' - lying on the floor reading 0.000m means the chip is ALIVE with an unusable sample, and must not be treated as broken.

nodes.label: cos(tilt) throttle feedforward compensation
nodes.rationale: Propeller thrust is always perpendicular to the BODY, so banking by theta leaves only F*cos(theta) vertical: 12 deg (MOVE_MAX_TILT_DEG) loses 2.2% (~22 duty on a ~1000 base), 15 deg loses 3.4%, 30 deg loses 13.4%. Without compensation the drone sinks whenever it banks. The Vz loop COULD absorb this through its I-term but takes several hundred ms to learn, by which time the drone has already dropped - cos compensation is FEEDFORWARD and is correct on the first tick. TILT_COMP_MAX_FACTOR = 1.10 is MANDATORY because 1/cos diverges as theta approaches 90 deg: a single bad attitude estimate (and it DOES go bad during collisions or heavy vibration) would yield an enormous factor and FULL THROTTLE. That ceiling is the only thing standing between a sensor error and maximum throttle; 1.10 covers up to ~24.6 deg, double the practical 12 deg flight limit. Compensation applies only when throttle_cmd > 0 - multiplying 0 stays 0 anyway, but the condition is explicit so nobody later accidentally 'revives' throttle after a disarm, landing cutoff or abort.
